title: Regulatory compliance checklist, by state and city

slides.title: Legal is a written decision for one address and one plan
slides.subtitle: Resource SR.1. Regulatory compliance checklist, by state and city
meta: Alder Street unit and Cedar Ridge house (hypothetical)
Education only. Not legal, tax, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
This resource is the sheet you fill in before you sign a lease or make an offer. It ends in one of three words: permitted, prohibited, or unresolved. Every answer on it points to an official page, a date, and the person who checked it.

I'll walk you through each section of the template and the rules that decide the result. Then we run two tests. We drop the Alder Street unit into New York City, and then into Los Angeles. After that we look at Cedar Ridge, where almost every line is still blank, because that's what day one of due diligence looks like.

One thing to hold onto the whole way through. I'm teaching a method. I'm not your attorney, and nothing on these slides says a specific address is legal. The checklist helps you ask the right questions and write down the answers. A local professional still confirms the decision.

slides.title: Rules attach to the address and your plan, so neighbors can get different answers

left.head: What the sheet does
items: Turns "is this legal?" into a written decision for one exact address
Ends in permitted, prohibited, or unresolved
Shows the official page behind every answer
Records who checked each line, when, and what still needs a professional

right.head: What it does not do
items: Rate a whole state or city as "legal" or "Airbnb-friendly"
Show you where to click. Sam's 3.2 and PA.2 do that
Replace a local attorney's review of the decision

box.label: Bring back from Sam's 3.2 and PA.2
box.text: Sam shows you where to click. This sheet is where you write down what you found and what you decided.

slides.notes:
Here's the idea the whole sheet is built on. Rules attach to the address, the building, the zoning district, the permit category, and your plan for the unit. They don't attach to a city in general. Two units on the same street can get different answers.

So this sheet never rates a state or a city as legal or Airbnb-friendly. It gives you a written decision for one exact address and one exact plan, with the official page behind every line.

It sits next to two of Sam's lessons. In 3.2, How to Research Regulations Before You Sign Anything, he runs the live search. Owners use it with his PA.2 when they screen markets. Don't expect this deck to repeat those demos. Watch Sam find the pages. Then come back here and write down what you found, the date, and what you decided.

slides.title: Work the seven sections top to bottom, because each one feeds the next
rows: Hosted or unhosted, whole unit or room, stay length, maximum guests, who lives there
State, county, city, zoning, building, HOA, lease, insurance. Each with URL, date, result, reviewer
Category, prerequisites, caps, primary-residence test, renewal, transfer, safety, ad rules
Each registration and who remits on each channel. Federal income tax stays with your CPA
Anything unclear goes to the office in writing. Save the reply as a dated PDF
Every open item gets an owner and a due date
The decision, the reason, and a recheck date
slides.notes:
The order matters. You start with the plan in Section A, because most rules turn on those facts. Is the host there during the stay? Is it the whole unit or a room? How long do guests stay, how many of them, and who lives there the rest of the year? A vague plan gives you a vague answer.

Then Section B walks each layer of permission, from the state down to your lease and your insurance. Section C records the permit details. Section D records tax registrations and who remits on each channel. Keep permit registration and tax registration apart. They're separate filings.

E, F, and G close the loop. Anything unclear goes out as a written question. Anything still open gets an owner and a due date. Then you apply the decision rules and write the result, the reason, and a recheck date.

slides.title: Each line needs an official source, the quoted sentence, a date, and a reviewer
items: Use official sources for rules: city, county, and state pages, the adopted ordinance, the tax agency
Paste the sentence that decides the case into the Result cell, with the URL beside it
Date every check. Rules change, and a result without a date is a guess
Name a reviewer. "Self" works for a first pass. Deciding lines get a second reviewer, such as a local STR attorney
Save evidence as PDFs and screenshots in one folder named with the address

box.label: Platform pages
box.text: A platform help page tells you what the platform does, such as which taxes it collects. Airbnb's own [regulations overview](https://www.airbnb.com/resources/hosting-homes/a/learn-about-hosting-regulations-7) calls itself a starting point. The city decides what it allows.

slides.notes:
These five habits are what make the sheet worth trusting.

First, official sources only for rules. That means the city, county, and state pages, the adopted ordinance, and the tax agency. A platform page can tell you what the platform does. Airbnb says its own regulations overview is a starting point, so treat it that way.

Second, quote the line that decides the case. Don't paraphrase it. Paste the sentence and put the URL right beside it. When your attorney reads the sheet, they can check your reading in a few seconds.

Third, date everything. Fourth, name a reviewer. "Self" is fine on a first pass. Any line that decides the deal should also show a second person, such as a local short-term rental attorney.

Last, save the evidence. One folder, named with the address, holding PDFs of each page, portal screenshots, and any written replies.

slides.title: Apply the five decision rules in order and stop at the first one that fits

gates.q: Does any official source clearly bar the planned use at this address?
gates.sub: Example: the plan is unhosted and the city allows only hosted stays

gates.q: Do the lease, HOA, condo, or building rules bar short stays, or is written landlord permission missing?
Is a required permit capped, closed, or unavailable to your type of operator?
gates.sub: Example: permits can't transfer to a new operator
gates.no: Prohibited for now; note when it reopens

gates.q: Is any deciding line blank, "to verify", or resting only on a platform page or a verbal answer?

slides.end: Rule 5. Every deciding line has an official source dated within 90 days, a written answer where the source was unclear, and no open item that could change it: **Permitted** for this plan, with its conditions.
slides.notes:
Section G takes one of three answers, and these rules pick it. Go in order. Stop at the first rule that fits.

Rule 1 is the city, county, or state saying no to this plan. Rule 2 is the private layer: the lease, the HOA, the condo documents, or the building rules. If the landlord hasn't given written permission, that's a no until they do. Rule 3 is the permit itself. It might be capped or closed. Or it might not be open to someone like you, for example when permits can't pass to a new operator.

Rule 4 catches the gaps. A blank line, a "to verify", or a line that rests on a platform page or on something someone told you on the phone. That's unresolved.

Only when all of that clears do you reach Rule 5 and write permitted. Notice how much Rule 5 asks for. Official source, dated within 90 days, a written answer where the page was unclear, and nothing open that could flip it.

slides.title: Unresolved means don't sign, and permitted covers only the plan in Section A
items: Change the plan (more guests, more nights, a different stay length) and you rerun the sheet
On an unresolved address you can keep negotiating. You don't sign a lease, release a deposit, or waive a contingency
A prohibited result can point to a different plan, such as stays of 30 nights or more. That's a different business, so start a new sheet

box.label: Recheck dates
box.text: Recheck 90 days after the decision (assumption: a teaching default; go shorter if the city has a pending ordinance), and again 30 days before any permit renewal.

slides.notes:
Three more rules keep the decision honest.

A permitted result only covers the plan you wrote in Section A. If you later decide to add a bed, take more guests, or rent more nights, you've changed the plan. Rerun the sheet.

Unresolved is the answer people try to talk themselves past. Here's the line. You can keep talking to the landlord or the seller. You don't sign the lease, you don't release a deposit, and you don't waive a contingency while the sheet says unresolved.

And prohibited isn't always the end. Some cities treat stays of 30 nights or more differently from short stays. That's a different business, with a different lease clause and different numbers, so it gets its own sheet.

On the recheck: I use 90 days as a teaching default. If the city has an ordinance in the works, check sooner. Always check again 30 days before a permit renewal.

slides.title: Most rules turn on the plan, so Section A pins it down before any research
rows: City, or unincorporated county; special districts
County GIS or city boundary map
Code on the official zoning map
Who lives there, months per year
Hosted or unhosted; whole unit or rooms
Typical and minimum nights; maximum guests
Nights per year; Airbnb, Vrbo, Booking.com, direct
slides.caption: Status takes one of four values: Done, Written answer, To verify, or N/A with a reason.
slides.notes:
Section A is the part people skip, and it's the part everything else depends on.

The top half pins down the property. Address and unit, the parcel number from the assessor, and whether you're inside a city or in unincorporated county. Then the zoning district, off the official zoning map. Year built can matter too, because rent-control coverage turns on it in some cities.

The bottom half is your plan. Does anyone live there as a primary residence? Is the host present? Whole unit or rooms? How long do guests stay, how many can sleep there, how many nights a year, and on which channels?

The Status column keeps you honest. Done means an official source, dated. Written answer means you have a reply from the office saved. To verify means you don't know yet. N/A needs a reason next to it. Fill this in once, and every later section reads off it.

slides.title: Section B checks ten layers of permission, and any one of them can stop the deal
slides.text: Fill every column for each row: official source URL, date checked, a one-sentence result with the quoted line, and the reviewer.
rows: STR law, lodging-tax registration, any preemption of local rules
STR ordinance if unincorporated; county lodging tax
STR or registration law; definitions of STR, host, primary residence
Permitted, conditional, or prohibited use in this district
Building class, prohibited-building lists, fire and occupancy rules
Is the unit covered by rent control or stabilization?
CC&Rs, bylaws, minimum lease terms, rental caps
Written permission, sublet clause, guest rules
Covers short-term guests at this address
Mortgage allows the use; occupancy covenant
slides.notes:
Section B is where most deals get decided. There are ten layers, and a no on any one of them stops the plan.

The first six are government layers. The state may have its own law, or may limit what cities can do. The county matters if the parcel sits outside city limits. The city has the ordinance and its definitions, and definitions matter. What counts as a host, or a primary residence, can decide your case. Then zoning, the building, and whether the unit is under rent regulation.

The last four are private. The HOA or condo documents. Your lease, with written permission, which lesson 5.3 covers. Your insurer, in writing, which 2.4 covers. And for owners, the loan documents.

For the HOA row, you won't find a government page. Write down where you got the documents. Every row still gets a date, a result with the quoted line, and a reviewer.

slides.title: Permit and tax registrations are separate filings, so they get separate sections

left.head: Section C. Permit details
items: Category that fits the Section A plan, and the issuing office
Prerequisites, fee, and term
Caps, waitlist, and the primary-residence test
Renewal, and whether a new operator can use the permit
Local contact, safety rules, permit number in ads, penalties

right.head: Section D. Taxes by channel
right.note: Lesson 3.3 covers this in depth. Federal income tax is a CPA question.
items: Registration number and agency for each tax
Rate and base: does it include cleaning fees?
Does Airbnb collect it? Does Vrbo?
Direct bookings: the operator collects and remits
Filing frequency, and whether zero returns are due

slides.notes:
Section C is the permit itself. Name the category that fits your plan, not just "the STR permit". Then the prerequisites, the fee, and how long it lasts. Caps and waitlists go here, and so does the primary-residence test, with the exact definition and the proof it needs. Transferability is the one owners miss. Does the permit stay with the owner, the host, or the property? Can a new operator use it?

Section D is taxes, and it runs by channel. A platform may collect some taxes and not others. You may still need to register and file returns even when a platform remits. On direct bookings, you collect and remit. Write down each tax, the agency, the rate, whether cleaning fees are in the base, and how often you file.

Lesson 3.3 teaches occupancy tax properly. Here you're only recording it. And keep federal income tax out of this sheet. That's a conversation with your CPA.

slides.title: Sections E to G turn open questions into owners, due dates, and a dated decision
slides.text: Section E logs each written question with the rule quoted and the reply saved. Section F gives every open item an owner, a due date, and a yes or no on whether it blocks the decision. Section G:
rows: Night caps, guest caps, renewal date, posting rules
Decision date + 90 days, and 30 days before permit renewal
slides.notes:
The last three sections are short, and they're where the sheet earns its keep.

Section E is your written questions. For each one, quote the rule you're asking about, note who you sent it to and when, and paste the answer when it comes back. Save the reply as a PDF.

Section F is the open list. Every item gets a person who clears it: you, your attorney, your CPA, your insurer, your lender, or the licensing office. It gets a due date. And it gets a yes or no on one question: could this item change the decision?

Section G is the decision. Write which of the three results you reached and which rule got you there. Add one sentence of reason with its source. If it's permitted, list the conditions, like night caps and posting rules. Then the names, the date, and the recheck date. Someone else should be able to read this row and see exactly why you decided what you did.

slides.title: Write the Alder Street plan first: an unhosted whole unit, 5 guests, 255 nights
rows: 218 Alder Street, Unit 4B (placed in NYC, then LA, for these tests)
Four-unit residential building, leased from a small landlord
slides.notes:
Now let's use it. Alder Street is our hypothetical two-bedroom, two-bath apartment, Unit 4B, in a four-unit building leased from a small landlord. It sleeps 5. The canonical example leaves the city unnamed on purpose. That lets us drop the same unit into two real cities and see how the answer changes.

Here's the plan, written first. The operator doesn't live there. Nobody is on site during stays. Guests rent the whole unit. Stays average 3.0 nights. Up to 5 guests. 255 booked nights a year, on Airbnb and Vrbo. All of those numbers are assumptions from the example.

Look at how specific that is. Every one of these facts is something a city rule can turn on. Host present or not. Whole unit or room. Guest count. Nights per year. Primary residence. With this written down, the research in Section B has something exact to test against.

slides.title: In NYC, Alder Street fails at Section B on host presence and the two-guest limit
columns: Result from the official OSE page
rows: Local Law 18 of 2022: renting for fewer than 30 consecutive days requires OSE registration
Host must be present for stays under 30 days; no renting an entire apartment or home
No more than two paying guests (children under 4 not counted)
A natural person who is the permanent occupant of the unit
Platforms may not process transactions for unregistered short-term rentals
Rent-regulated and NYCHA units can't register; $145 non-refundable fee
The city rule already fails the plan
slides.caption: Checked 2026-09-25 by official-domain search of nyc.gov; pages not opened directly. Open them yourself. Real use needs an NYC attorney as second reviewer.
slides.notes:
First test: New York City. The city's Mayor's Office of Special Enforcement, OSE, runs registration under Local Law 18 of 2022. Anyone renting housing for fewer than 30 consecutive days has to register.

Then the plan runs into three rules at once. OSE says the host has to be present for stays under 30 days, and you can't rent an entire apartment or home. It caps stays at two paying guests. And the person registering has to be a natural person who permanently lives in the unit. Alder Street is unhosted, whole unit, 5 guests, and the operator lives elsewhere. It fails on every one.

Platforms also can't process bookings for unregistered rentals, so this isn't a rule you can quietly ignore.

Notice the rows marked not reached. I didn't research the lease or insurance, because the city rule already ended it. One caution: these checks came from official-domain search, not from opening the pages. Open them yourself before you rely on any of this.

slides.title: In Los Angeles, the same plan fails on primary residence and the 120-day cap
rows: Adopted December 2018. Limits STRs to the host's primary residence
Signed declaration that the host lives there more than six months a year
Standard Home-Sharing allows up to 120 days a year
RSO units can't be used. RSO covers most non-single-family rentals built before October 1, 1978
Written, notarized landlord approval filed with the registration
A draft Vacation Rental Ordinance exists; search did not show it adopted
FAQ states $89 per registration or renewal, renewed yearly
slides.caption: Checked 2026-09-25 by official-domain search of planning.lacity.gov, housing.lacity.gov, and finance.lacity.gov. Real use needs a Los Angeles attorney.
slides.notes:
Same unit, same plan, now inside the City of Los Angeles.

LA's Home-Sharing Ordinance, adopted in December 2018, limits short-term rental to the host's primary residence. The host signs a declaration saying they live there more than six months of the year. Our operator lives elsewhere, so the plan fails right there.

It would fail a second way too. Standard Home-Sharing allows up to 120 days a year. Our plan is 255 nights.

A few lines stay open, and I've marked them to verify. The Rent Stabilization Ordinance covers most non-single-family rentals built before October 1, 1978, so a four-unit building needs its year built checked. City Planning has published a draft ordinance for non-primary residences, and the search didn't show it as adopted. The FAQ lists an $89 fee, but that document may be older than the current fee schedule.

Those open lines don't change today's answer. They're what you'd ask the city about in writing.

slides.title: In LA, Airbnb remits the 14% city TOT, but the host still registers and files monthly
slides.text: Section D is filled here to show how it works, even though the plan already fails Section B.
rows: TOT Registration Certificate from the LA Office of Finance, within 30 days of starting
14% of rent, for stays of 30 days or less
Collects and remits city TOT. Airbnb's article says the base includes cleaning fees
To verify in Vrbo's tax pages
Monthly return, due by the 25th of the following month. Host files and deducts platform-remitted tax
slides.caption: Sources: [LA Office of Finance: TOT requirements](https://finance.lacity.gov/transient-occupancy-tax-requirements); [Airbnb: California collection](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2297). Checked 2026-09-25.
slides.notes:
I filled Section D for Los Angeles even though the plan fails, so you can see how the section reads.

The city Transient Occupancy Tax is 14% of rent for stays of 30 days or less. You register with the LA Office of Finance and get a TOT Registration Certificate within 30 days of starting.

Now the part people get wrong. Airbnb collects and remits the city TOT on Airbnb bookings, and its article says the base includes cleaning fees. That doesn't mean you're finished. The host still files a monthly return, due by the 25th of the next month, and deducts what the platform already remitted. Vrbo's handling is marked to verify. On direct bookings, you collect and remit it all yourself.

That's why this section has a column per channel. The same tax can be handled three different ways depending on where the guest booked. Lesson 3.3 goes deeper on this.

slides.title: Both cities say prohibited, for reasons a note like "legal with a permit" would miss
rows: Host presence, whole unit, 5 guests against a two-guest limit
Primary residence; 255 nights against the 120-day cap
Test a 30-night-plus furnished rental on a new sheet
Ask City Planning in writing about the draft ordinance
2026-12-24, or sooner if Local Law 18 changes

box.label: Why the plan comes first
box.text: The NYC test ends at Section B. You don't spend a week on tax rates for a use the city bars.

slides.notes:
Put the two decisions side by side. Both say prohibited under Rule 1. But the reasons are different.

New York fails the plan on host presence and guest count. Los Angeles fails it on primary residence and nights. If you'd written "LA: legal with a permit" in a notes file, you'd have missed both of those conditions.

Each decision also points somewhere. In New York, a prohibited short-stay plan can lead to a different plan, a furnished rental of 30 nights or more. That's a new sheet, a new lease clause, and new numbers. In Los Angeles, the open question is whether the draft ordinance for non-primary homes has been adopted. You ask City Planning in writing.

Both get a recheck date of December 24, 2026, which is 90 days after the September 25 decision. And look at how short the New York test was. That's what writing the plan first buys you.

slides.title: Most wrong answers come from a city label, a vague plan, or an unquoted source
items: Writing a city label, like "LA: legal with a permit", instead of a decision for one address and plan
Researching before Section A is written, so the answer is as vague as the plan
Treating a platform help page or a phone call as the final word on what the city allows
Paraphrasing the rule instead of pasting the sentence that decides it, with the URL
Leaving a result undated, or a deciding line with no second reviewer
Signing, releasing a deposit, or waiving a contingency while the sheet says unresolved
slides.notes:
Here are six mistakes to look for on any sheet, including your own.

The first one we just saw. A city label hides the conditions that actually decide your case. The second is starting research before the plan is written. If you don't know your guest count or whether you'll be on site, you can't tell whether a rule applies.

Third, a platform page or a phone call is not the final word. Platform pages are useful starting points. Phone calls are useful for finding the right office. Neither clears a deciding line.

Fourth, paraphrasing. Your summary of a rule is a claim. The quoted sentence with its link is evidence. Fifth, undated lines and no second reviewer on the lines that matter.

And the last one is the expensive one. Signing a lease or waiving a contingency while the sheet still says unresolved.

slides.title: Cedar Ridge is unresolved under Rule 4, and Section F lists the answers it needs
slides.text: Three-bed house in a drive-to lake market. Sleeps 8, no HOA, unhosted, 3.5-night stays, 212 nights, about 10 personal days a year. The example names no state or county, so every rule line is blank.
rows: Zoning use for STR at this parcel
Planning or licensing office, in writing
Permit transfer on sale, or new-application wait
Lender occupancy covenant fits 10 personal days
slides.caption: Action: keep the offer's regulatory and inspection contingencies open until items 1, 2, 4, and 5 have written answers.
slides.notes:
Cedar Ridge shows you what a sheet looks like on day one of due diligence. It's the hypothetical three-bedroom lake house that Maya and Chris would buy. It sleeps 8, has no HOA, and they'd use it about 10 days a year. The plan is unhosted, 3.5-night stays, 212 nights a year.

The canonical example doesn't name a state or county, so every rule line is blank. That gives us Rule 4: unresolved.

An unresolved sheet is still useful. It tells you exactly which emails to send and which contingency dates matter. Zoning and permit transfer have to be answered in writing before the contingency deadline. The lender has to confirm the occupancy covenant fits 10 personal days before the rate lock. The insurer confirms before closing.

Item 3, taxes, doesn't block the decision. It doesn't change whether the use is legal. It still has to be done before the first booking. PA.1 and Sam's PA.2 cover screening the market before you get this far.

slides.title: Email one topic at a time, quote the rule, and ask for the answer in writing
slides.text: Give the address, parcel, zoning district, the page you read with its date, and your exact plan. Then ask:
items: Is this use allowed at this parcel? Which permit or registration category applies?
Is there a cap, waitlist, or pending change that affects a new application?
If the property is sold, does the permit transfer, or must the buyer apply again?
Which safety inspection and local-contact rules apply?
Which lodging-tax registrations does your office or another office require?

box.label: A phone answer is not enough
box.text: A call helps you find the right office. It doesn't clear a deciding line under Rule 5. Ask the person to confirm by email.

slides.notes:
When an official page doesn't answer a deciding question, you write to the office. The full sample email is in SR.1.7. Here's how it's built.

Open with the facts: the full address, the parcel number, the zoning district, and the page you read, with the date. Then state your plan in one short paragraph. Whole unit or room, hosted or not, average stay, guests, nights a year, whether it's your primary residence, and whether you own or lease.

Then ask the five questions on the slide, and ask for the answer in writing. Offices answer faster when they can reply yes, no, or see section X. If another office handles part of it, ask them to tell you which one.

When the reply comes in, paste the key sentence into Section E, save the email as a PDF, and update the Status column. And if someone gives you a good answer on the phone, thank them and ask them to put it in an email.

slides.title: The attorney confirms the decision, and four other parties confirm their own lines
rows: The decision is right for this address, this plan, and this lease or contract
In writing: permit category, caps, transferability, any pending ordinance
Which lodging-tax registrations you need and what each platform remits
In writing: the policy covers short-term guests at this address
In writing: short-term stays are allowed
slides.caption: Hand over the filled sheet and the evidence folder. Any line that decides the deal should show a second reviewer.
slides.notes:
This is how you hand the sheet to the professionals. Bring the whole thing, plus the evidence folder, so they can check your sources instead of starting over.

The local short-term rental attorney confirms the decision itself: that it's right for this address, this plan, and this lease or purchase contract. That's the second reviewer on your deciding lines.

The licensing or planning office confirms the permit facts in writing. The category, caps, whether a permit transfers, and anything pending. The state, county, and city tax agencies, along with your CPA, confirm which lodging-tax registrations you need and what each platform remits.

Your insurer confirms in writing that short-term guests are covered at this address. And the private layer confirms in writing too. For arbitrage that's your landlord. For ownership it's the HOA, if there is one, and your lender.

Each person confirms their own piece. Nobody confirms all of it.

box.label: Owners in STR Concierge
box.text: Run the sheet on each finalist market during Sam's PA.2, then again on the exact parcel before the offer's contingencies expire.

slides.notes:
Here's where the sheet shows up in the course.

In the Roadmap, fill Section A after lesson 3.1, once you know how licensing, zoning, and primary-residence rules work. Run Sections B and C while you watch Sam's 3.2 live search. Complete Section D with lesson 3.3 on occupancy taxes. Then lesson 3.4 uses your Section G result as the first gate of its reject, investigate, or advance screen.

Owners in STR Concierge use it twice. First on each finalist market during Sam's PA.2, as a screen. Then again on the exact parcel, before the offer's contingencies run out. The market-level pass tells you where to look. The parcel-level pass is the one that decides.

After a unit clears this sheet, SR.5 picks up. That's where you choose the tools that will show the permit number in your listings and route taxes by channel.

slides.title: Start one real sheet this week and get one deciding line to Done
items: Copy Section A and write the plan for one real address: hosting, whole unit or room, stay length, guests, nights
Find the city's STR ordinance on an official site. Paste the deciding sentence into Section B with the URL and today's date
Make one evidence folder named with the address, and save each page you used as a PDF
Draft the SR.1.7 email for one deciding question the official page doesn't answer, and send it
slides.next: Next: SR.5 Tool comparison guide: PMS, dynamic pricing, AI guest messaging. It picks up once a unit clears this sheet.
slides.notes:
Four things for this week, and none of them should take more than an hour.

Pick one real address you're looking at and write Section A. Be specific about the plan. If you haven't decided the guest count or whether you'll be on site, decide now, because the research depends on it.

Then find the city's short-term rental ordinance on an official site. Not a blog, and not a platform page. Paste the one sentence that decides your case into Section B, with the link and today's date.

Set up the evidence folder, named with the address, and save the pages you used as PDFs.

Last, find one deciding question that the page doesn't answer, and send the email from SR.1.7. Then you'll have a written answer coming.

When a unit clears the sheet, move to SR.5, the tool comparison guide. That's where the permit number and your tax routing turn into software settings.

These are the main sources behind the slides. The full list, with how each was checked, is in the SR.1 sources section of the resource.

Two things to know about them. First, every rule check was done on September 25, 2026, by searching the official domains, not by opening every page. So open each page yourself before you rely on it, and put your own date on your own sheet.

Second, notice which sources decide things and which don't. The NYC and LA pages are the rules. The Airbnb pages tell you what Airbnb does, such as requiring a permit number before a listing goes live. Airbnb's own regulations page calls itself a starting point.

Rules change. The LA draft ordinance is the clearest example on this list. That's why every sheet carries a recheck date.
